headline: Stop watching named protocols; drag elements onto a workbench where laws light missing parts and hazards flare until the set coheres or breaks.

concepts.name: Protocol Workbench
concepts.signature_moment: You drop Pooled Lending; three requirement sockets bloom empty, then snap shut green as you fill Claim + Exit Liquidity—then a hazard edge flares red when you add the wrong collateral.
concepts.what_happens: A docked half-plane workbench sits under the depth rows. Drag an element tile from the atlas (or long-press then fling) onto the bench; it settles in ~280ms with a soft thud. Within 120ms, each law whose left side is now satisfied sprouts hollow socket chips labeled by family alternatives (e.g. Sh|Ix). Fulfilled sockets fill and desaturate; unfilled pulse once then hold a dim notch. Hazard rules whose full left-hand set is present draw a short red chord between the offending tiles and stamp a one-line hazard chip. A completeness meter (0–100%) ticks as law coverage rises. Empty bench = no sockets.
concepts.why_this_data: The 29 laws are already a directed graph with OR choice points; 19 hazard rules name forbidden co-presence. Depth S0–S4 and family substitutes define valid socket fill. This is the atlas's requirement algebra made tactile—not generic drag-and-drop tagging.
concepts.user_action: Drag tiles onto/off the workbench; click a socket chip to filter the atlas to only that family's candidates; optional 'seed from protocol' loads a real stack as a starting hand.
concepts.they_now_understand: That a protocol is a closure under requirements, not a bag of features—and which substitute families are interchangeable at each choice point.
concepts.displaces: Click-a-name-and-watch protocol fly-in as the primary way to learn composition.
concepts.failure_mode: Socket spam on large sets; mitigations: only show laws newly activated by last drop, collapse fulfilled sockets, cap simultaneous hollow chips to three with '+N more'.

concepts.name: What-If Diff
concepts.signature_moment: You yank the oracle out of a loaded protocol; three dependents go ghost-hollow in sequence along the law chain, and a dead protocol's death tag glows if that exact hole matches how it died.
concepts.what_happens: Load any of the 12 protocols as a sealed cluster on the workbench (numbered 1..n in causal order, still). Grab one member and drag it off; over ~400ms the cluster reflows: remaining tiles hold place, removed tile leaves a dashed silhouette. Laws that lost a required dependency light the dependents with a brief inward-collapse (scale 1→0.92→1, 200ms) and a 'broken by: …' chip. If the residual set matches a known failure pattern (reflexive loop / self-thin collateral), that death annotation slides in from the margin. Put the piece back and the damage reverse-plays.
concepts.why_this_data: Protocols are ordered subsets; deaths are labeled structural failures; laws are the dependency edges. Removing a node is only meaningful because requirements and corpse-cases exist in the data.
concepts.user_action: Seed a real protocol, then pull pieces out or swap a family substitute in; toggle 'show only broken laws'.
concepts.they_now_understand: Why each later part was forced—and which single missing part would have made the same corpse.
concepts.displaces: Passive numbered highlight of protocol members with no counterfactual.
concepts.failure_mode: Death matches that feel forced or false-positive; only fire when residual set is a known subset of a documented failure, never fuzzy.

concepts.name: Turn-Over Card
concepts.signature_moment: You flip Atomic Flash Liquidity; the back shows a single red stamp—async-impossible—while the front's neighbors dim to the three things that cannot share its time model.
concepts.what_happens: Click-and-hold (or keyboard Enter) on a focused tile: it rotates 180° on Y over 320ms (CSS 3D on the DOM card). Face shows name/family/depth; back shows asynchrony (native / repairable / impossible), status (core/candidate/contested/degenerate-limit), and a compact 'required by N laws / requires M' count. Releasing or pressing again flips back and settles. Reduced-motion: instant face swap, same content. While face-down, a thin WebGL or SVG non-text layer draws requirement stubs only for this element's incident laws—no ambient motion.
concepts.why_this_data: Asynchrony is a three-way property with one extreme singleton; status and law in/out-degree are element-native fields. The flip reveals attributes the flat labels omit without inventing new taxonomy.
concepts.user_action: Pick up one tile at a time and turn it over; arrow keys walk neighbors while keeping the back face.
concepts.they_now_understand: The hidden axes—especially that one element is structurally async-impossible—and how dense its law neighborhood is.
concepts.displaces: Tooltip/detail panel as the only 'inspect' path.
concepts.failure_mode: Flip fights text selection; gate flip on intentional hold >150ms or a dedicated flip control so copy-paste still works.

concepts.name: Assembly Race
concepts.signature_moment: Clock hits zero: your bench has a closed law set but one red hazard chord—you win 'coherent but cursed'; a friend wins clean and slower.
concepts.what_happens: Optional timed mode (3 or 10 minutes). Goal card drawn from real protocol shapes or abstract law closures (e.g. 'stand up leveraged yield without an elevated hazard'). Palette is the full 59; workbench sockets and hazard chords update live as in Protocol Workbench. Score = law-closure completeness − hazard penalties − unnecessary depth bloat. End screen shows your set beside the nearest real protocol subset (Jaccard on elements) and names the first unsatisfied law. Shareable seed string encodes the goal + RNG. No perpetual camera motion—only discrete chip updates.
concepts.why_this_data: Goals are literally law-closure problems with OR alternatives and hazard penalties unique to this graph; nearest-protocol match uses the 12 real subsets. Untimed workbench is the practice mode; race is the same algebra under pressure.
concepts.user_action: Start a round, drag-build under a goal constraint, submit or auto-score at timeout.
concepts.they_now_understand: Trade-offs: speed vs hazard-free closure, and how close their invention sits to shipped systems.
concepts.displaces: Browse-only sessions for users who already 'got' the table in thirty seconds.
concepts.failure_mode: Feels gimmicky if goals are arbitrary; seed every goal from a real law cluster or a known protocol minus two parts so answers exist.

concepts.name: Substitute Swapper
concepts.signature_moment: You spin the claim-record socket through Share→Index receipt; the rest of the stack stays put while only the family slot morphs, and a hazard that cared about Share vanishes.
concepts.what_happens: On a workbench (or protocol-seeded) set, each law socket that admits | alternatives becomes a horizontal reel. Drag sideways or click chevrons: the current family member slides out (120ms) and the next substitute slides in. Only tiles in that family cycle; dependents do not move. Hazard chords recompute on each detent. A small 'N of M substitutes' counter sits under the reel.
concepts.why_this_data: Families are defined as mutual substitutes answering the same design question; laws encode (A|B|C) choice points. Swapping inside a family is the atlas's core claim made into a control.
concepts.user_action: Focus a socket or family-tagged tile and scrub substitutes without rebuilding the whole stack.
concepts.they_now_understand: Which parts are load-bearing vs interchangeable—and that 'different protocol' often means one family swap, not a new invention.
concepts.displaces: Re-selecting whole protocols to compare near-variants.
concepts.failure_mode: Users cycle into contested/degenerate members without noticing; mark status on the reel tooth so degenerate options look notched.

the_one_to_build: Protocol Workbench — it turns the unused law graph and hazard rules into a direct-manipulation game loop and is the substrate What-If Diff, Substitute Swapper, and Assembly Race all sit on.
what_everyone_will_get_wrong: They will invent prettier ways to watch a pre-authored protocol fly into place, instead of letting the user assemble under the laws and feel requirements and hazards as feedback.
